newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican government acts to put brakes on peso.
newsitem.headline: Mexican government acts to put brakes on peso.

text.p: Faced with robust capital flows into Mexico, the government has made a move to slow further appreciation of the peso.

The Exchange Commission -- made up of officials from Banco de Mexico and the Finance Ministry -- said late Wednesday it would almost double the dollar put options to be auctioned for August. But the move to rebuild international reserves and put a brake on the appreciation of the muscular peso may not be enough in the face of a soaring stock market and strong foreign direct investment, analysts said.
The bank has been auctioning dollar put options since mid-1996 in an attempt to rebuild its reserves.
The amount of the options has been increased to $500 million for August, for the first time, and with the possibility of a second auction. The previous auction was for $300 million.

"What has happened is that there is a strong offer of dollars, and when there is this offer we have to take advantage to accumulate reserves," a government official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters.
The Exchange Commission also said, in a rare reference to the level of the currency, that it was concerned the strong peso could harm the sustainability of the economic recovery.
It said in its statement that an "important" flow of funds could persist over the next few months as the economy recovers and good conditions in international financial markets continue.
"The action has both interpretations," the official said, adding that the Exchange Commission reserved the right to keep to the $500 million level at further auctions.
The central bank has exercised options for $3.26 billion in about a year. Net reserves were $22.51 billion on July 29.
The government has been under strong pressure to do something about the peso, as industry leaders and opposition politicians complain about the possibly overvalued currency.

Carlos Moreno Munoz, president of the Mexican Institute of Financial Executives, said the strength of the peso has caused a "red alert" over the risk of an abrupt economic correction, according to El Financiero newspaper on Thursday.
But the bull run on the Mexican bolsa -- it hit another record high on Wednesday before continuing its run on Thursday -- seems set to keep taking the peso along for the ride.

"What it (the put option rise) will do is curb potential nominal appreciation, but I am not really sure it will generate further depreciation," said IDEA economist Gene Frieda, calling the move a prudent attempt to use peso strength to build reserves.

The peso, widely expected to weaken in its familiar step-wise fashion after historic mid-term elections on July 6, has instead continued to appreciate, with some economists saying it is now about 10 percent overvalued. Some fund managers are also wondering if Mexico is heading for a fall.

"We have eliminated our peso exposure. The peso has been very strong and it has rallied almost seven or eight percent in real terms now. Mexico as a growing economy really cannot afford that kind of overvaluation," said one New York-based fund manager.

"You get back to that same situation that you had earlier, and I don't think anyone in this government in Mexico really wants to go through that again. It has taken them years to get out of that situation," the manager said.
